evidence_quotes.quote: All major projects must be approved by the central government.
also lack autonomy in setting realistic tariffs, which would help them recover costs
thousands of residents have been plagued by erratic water supply.

rationale: This qualitative desktop and key-informant interview/observation study (conducted across six urban councils and ZINWA from 2008 to 2012) diagnoses the causes and impacts of urban domestic water and sanitation failures in Zimbabwe. Among legal and governance mechanisms, the central empirical bottleneck analyzed is intergovernmental centralization and lack of municipal fiscal/operational autonomy (`institutional_structure_coordination`): urban councils depend on central government for capital infrastructure funding, must obtain central government approval for major projects, parts procurement, and tariff adjustments, and share fragmented responsibilities with ZINWA. Cost-recovery tariff constraints and metering/pricing rules (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`) and weak statutory pollution fines alongside municipal payment-default water disconnections (`enforcement_sanctions`) are secondary applicable mechanisms. The primary outcome analyzed throughout is `effective_access`—specifically severe service intermittency, daily/prolonged water rationing, declining water quantity and potability, collapsed sewage reticulation, reliance on unsafe shallow wells, and resulting water-borne disease outbreaks.
